faq.heading: What a plant manager asks first

items.q: What is a {ss}, exactly?
items.a: A production shift VKC runs on your line, on a shift your plant doesn’t cover. Our [lead hand](/glossary#lead-hand) directs it and our crew does the work; our QC sheets and production log document what ran. You buy the output, priced per unit or per shift, not the time.

items.q: What does {bn} cover?
items.a: Filling, labelling, [kitting](/glossary#kitting) and packing at our facility, plus toll blending to your formula when the product has to be made before it is packed. It is the overflow your line can’t absorb, handled under one roof.

items.q: Which products do you take?
items.a: Liquids and pastes from a handful of trades: cleaners, lubricants, sealers, coatings and colourants. If yours is close to one of those, ask; the container usually decides it.

items.q: What do you need to quote?
items.a: Four things: the product and how it pours, the container with its closure and label, the size and rhythm of the runs, and the date the first one ships. A [safety data sheet](/glossary#safety-data-sheet) helps.

items.q: How is the work priced?
items.a: {ss} is priced per unit or per shift. {bn} work is quoted on the job you describe: the product, the container, the count and the date. There is no rate card, because no two jobs run the same.

items.q: Can you come and look before quoting?
items.a: Yes. For {ss} a walkthrough of your line is how the quote gets made, since the shift is priced against what is actually on your floor. It is often the shorter path for {bn} work too.

items.q: What happens to what I send through the form?
items.a: It becomes one email to VKC, used to answer you. There is no database behind this site and no second copy: no advertising cookies, no trackers, nothing stored anywhere but the inbox it lands in.

body: A {ss} is a production shift that VKC runs for you. Before it starts, we agree on what it has to produce: the product, the container, the [specification](/glossary#specification) and the count. Then we run it, and what comes back to you is finished, packed product and the record of how it was made.
That is why it is priced per unit or per shift. The price follows the output, because the output is what you are buying.
The line stays yours. How the shift runs is ours.

items.q: Who makes the calls on the floor during the shift?
items.a: Our lead hand. From the first container to the last case, the shift is directed by our lead hand and run by our crew; the product, the line and the specification stay yours, and so does the last word on what the output has to be.

items.q: What do we get back the next morning?
items.a: Finished, packed product, counted, and the paperwork for the shift: our QC sheets and production log, filled in as it ran. If a lot needs explaining later, the explanation is already written down.

items.q: Does someone from our plant need to be there?
items.a: That is your call, not a condition. The shift does not depend on it: our lead hand directs it and our crew does the work on your line either way. Come and watch the first one if you want to see how it runs.

items.q: Which shift gets quoted?
items.a: The one your plant does not run. Say which on the form; the quote is made for that shift, per unit or per shift, and the walkthrough confirms what the line can do in it.

items.q: How is this different from adding people to our own roster?
items.a: You are not buying time on your floor; you are buying the shift’s output. The people on the line are VKC’s, directed by our lead hand, and what you pay for is what comes off the line, per unit or per shift, with the record to match. Nothing about how the shift is run lands on your desk.

contractPackaging.h1: Contract packaging for the overflow your line can’t absorb
contractPackaging.lead: When orders outrun your line, send the overflow to VKC. We fill it, label it, kit it and pack it at our facility, as a co-packer for liquids and pastes.

list: Filling, by weight or to a line on the container, whichever your product calls for.
Labelling.
Kitting: putting separate components together into one package.
Packing, so the product leaves ready to ship.
And [toll blending](/services/toll-blending), if the product has to be made before it is packed.

body: A bottleneck is the slowest step in a plant, the one everything else waits on. It is also the neck of the bottle we fill. {bn} works on both readings: it takes volume away from the step that is holding you back and puts it through our line instead.
These container families have already been through our line. If yours is not listed, tell us what it is.
The first thing we will ask is how thick your product is: water-thin, pourable, thick or paste. It decides how the product is filled, how fast, and which of our fill methods fits.

sections.h2: What to send for a quote
list: The product, and roughly how it runs.
The container and its closure.
Labels or kit components, if we are applying or assembling them.
Units per run, and how often you run.
When the first run has to ship.

items.q: What do we send you to start?
items.a: The product, or the formula if it still has to be made; the empty containers with their closures; the labels; and the spec the filled unit has to meet, with a [safety data sheet](/glossary#safety-data-sheet) if the product has one. If any of those is still being decided, say so, and the quote waits for it rather than guessing.

items.q: How do you check that each container holds the right amount?
items.a: By one of two fill methods, chosen for the product: weigh-fill, where the fill is set by weight, or fill-to-line, where it is set by the mark on the container. Which one applies is part of the quote.

items.q: Can you label and pack, or only fill?
items.a: All of it, under one quote: filling, labelling, [kitting](/glossary#kitting) when a product ships with components, and packing so the pallet leaves ready for the truck. You can also send only the step your line is short on, and keep the rest in house.

items.q: What if the product is not made yet?
items.a: Then it starts with [toll blending](/services/toll-blending): the batch is made here to your formula, and the fill follows in the same building. One quote covers both steps.

tollBlending.lead: You own the formula. We make the batch at our facility and, if you need it, fill and pack it there too.

body: Toll blending means we mix your product to your formula and your [specification](/glossary#specification). The formula is yours; the work of making the batch is ours.
The word is an old one: a toll is the fee paid to have your own material processed by someone else. You pay for the processing, and the product stays yours.
It suits a product that sells well enough to need more batches than you want to make yourself, or a new product you want made before you invest in equipment of your own.

{bn} puts blending, filling and packing at the same facility. A batch made here can go into bottles, jugs, pails or kits without another truck ride in between, with one quote and one place to call about it.
Cleaners, lubricants, sealers, coatings and colourants. Each behaves differently in a mixer and in a container; the industry pages say how.
list: [Cleaners](/industries/cleaners)
[Lubricants](/industries/lubricants)
[Sealers and coatings](/industries/sealers-and-coatings)

sections.h2: What we need to quote a blend
list: The formula, or enough about it to price the work.
The batch size you need, and how often.
How the finished product runs: water-thin, pourable, thick or paste.
How it should be packed, if we are packing it too.

items.q: Whose formula is it?
items.a: Yours. Toll blending is making your product to your formula; the formula stays yours to change, and the batch is made to it as written. What we need from it is enough to price and run the work.

items.q: Can the batch be filled here too?
items.a: Yes: that is the point of doing both at one facility. A batch made here goes straight into bottles, jugs, pails or kits, with one quote for the blend and the fill together.

items.q: How is a blend priced?
items.a: On the batch as described: what goes into it, how it has to be mixed and checked, its size and how often it comes around. Change any of those and the number changes with it.

items.q: Which products do you blend?
items.a: The same trades the fill line runs: cleaners and degreasers, lubricants and greases, sealers, coatings and colourants. A product close to one of those is worth asking about; how it behaves in the mixer decides it.

bottlesAndJugs.h1: Bottles and jugs for products that pour
bottlesAndJugs.lead: [HDPE](/glossary#hdpe) bottles and D-jugs carry most cleaners and many lubricants. Here are the ones that have already been through our line, and the two ways we fill them.

sections.h2: Bottles and jugs we have run
body: This list is a record of what we have filled, not a limit on what we will look at. If your bottle isn’t on it, send us its name or a sample.

[Weigh-fill](/glossary#weigh-fill) puts the same weight of product in every container. It suits a product sold by weight, and a product that foams, where the level is hard to read until the foam settles.

[Fill-to-line](/glossary#fill-to-line) brings every container to the same visible level. A row of bottles filled to the line looks even on a shelf, which matters when a buyer compares one bottle with the one beside it.
Which one fits is usually the product’s call, not ours. We’ll tell you which one we would use, and why.

A bottle is only finished once it is closed and labelled. So when you ask for a quote, the [closure](/glossary#closure) and the label are part of the question: what they are, who supplies them, and whether we are the ones putting them on.

list: The bottle or jug: its name, size and material, or a sample.
The closure it takes, and who supplies it.
The label, if we are applying it.
Whether the product foams, drips or strings when it pours.
Units per run, how often you run, and the date the first run ships.

body: If the product has to be made first, [toll blending](/services/toll-blending) happens in the same building as the fill. If the bottle is sold as part of a set, see [kits](/containers/kits). Heavier fills go in [pails](/containers/pails).

pails.h1: Pails for thick, heavy and industrial products
pails.lead: Plastic pails, metal pails and [Ropak](/glossary#ropak) containers are where thick products usually go: sealers, coatings, pastes, and lubricants sold by the pail.

body: Plastic, metal and Ropak, in the sizes listed below. If your pail is a different one, send us its name or a sample.
The container is usually chosen before it reaches us: by the product’s chemistry, by what your own customer expects, or by what your line already runs. We fill the one you sell in.
Thick products fill slowly and settle slowly. A paste doesn’t level itself in a pail the way a liquid does, so the surface can mislead anyone reading the fill by eye.
That is where [weigh-fill](/glossary#weigh-fill) earns its place: the scale reads the same weight whatever the surface looks like.

list: The pail: plastic, metal or Ropak, its size, and its lid.
The product, and how thick it is: pourable, thick or paste.
Whether it is sold by weight or by volume.
The label, if we are applying it.
How many pails a run, how often, and when the first one ships.

body: A pail often holds a product that was blended for the job. [Toll blending](/services/toll-blending) and filling happen at the same facility, so the batch doesn’t travel between them. Lighter products go in [bottles and jugs](/containers/bottles-and-jugs).

kits.h1: Consumer kits, assembled from your components
kits.lead: A kit is several products sold as one: a bottle and its brush, a sealer and its applicator, a set built for a store shelf. We put the pieces together into one finished package.

body: [Kitting](/glossary#kitting) means bringing separate components together in one package that sells as a single unit. The components can be filled products, accessories such as a brush or a cloth, and printed pieces such as an instruction sheet.
Consumer kits have already been through our facility. The list stays short on purpose: a kit is defined by what goes into it, and no two are alike.

A kit is hand assembly in a plant built for flow. It needs table space, a count of every component, and time the filling line can’t spare. Seasonal kits and promotional sets add a deadline on top. It is careful work, and a missing component comes back as a return. Sending the assembly out keeps your line on what it does best.

list: One finished kit, or a photo of one, as the reference.
The list of components, and who supplies each one.
The outer package the kit is sold in.
How the pieces sit in the package.
Kits per run, and the date they have to ship.

body: When a kit holds a product that also has to be filled, both jobs can happen at our facility: the [bottle](/containers/bottles-and-jugs) is filled, then goes straight into the kit. One quote, one delivery date, one number to call.

cleaners.h1: Cleaners, filled and blended to your formula
cleaners.lead: Degreasers, all-purpose cleaners, glass and floor cleaners, industrial soaps: water-based products that foam the moment they move, and that sell in bottles, jugs and pails.

sections.h2: Why cleaners are their own job
body: A cleaner is mostly water carrying something that works, and that something is usually a surfactant. At a filling line it has one consequence above all others: it foams. Move it, drop it, splash it, and it throws a head of foam that hides the real level in the container.
So the fill slows down, or the container is weighed instead of read by eye, or both. None of that is a problem. It just has to be known before the first container goes under the head.

A concentrate and its ready-to-use version are two different jobs. The concentrate is a shorter run of a thicker, stronger product, often in a pail. The ready-to-use version is a longer run of mostly water, in a bottle with a trigger or a cap. Same formula on paper, different work on the floor.
Tell us which one you are quoting, or both, and how the volume splits between them.
Bottles and jugs for what goes on a shelf; pails for concentrate and for what a plant buys for its own use.

sections.h2: Two ways we can take the work
body: If your own line is the constraint, [{ss}](/services/second-shift) runs it on a shift your plant doesn’t cover. If the line is full, the overflow comes to us instead.
If the batch has to be made as well as packed, [toll blending](/services/toll-blending) happens in the same building as the fill.

sections.h2: What to send for a quote
list: The safety data sheet, so we know what we are handling.
Whether it is a concentrate or ready to use.
The container, the closure and the label.
How much it foams when it is poured.
Run size, frequency, and the date the first batch has to be out.

lubricants.h1: Lubricants, from light oils to grease
lubricants.lead: Motor and machine oils, hydraulic and cutting fluids, greases: products sold by the litre or by the pail, which behave nothing like water at a filling head.

body: An oil fills slower than a cleaner and drains slower off the nozzle. A grease barely flows at all; it has to be pushed. Most of what a lubricant blender sells sits somewhere between those two, and where a product sits decides how the fill is set up.

Temperature has a say too. A litre of warm oil weighs less than a litre of cold oil, because oil takes up more room as it warms. When the number on the label has to be exact, that is an argument for filling by weight.

A lubricant leaves a film behind. What ran before yours matters, and so does what follows it. Tell us what your product must not meet (a colour, an additive, a base oil) and we will work out the order and the cleanup with you.
Jugs and bottles for shelf sizes, pails for shop and plant sizes.

sections.h2: Two ways we can take the work
body: If the blending is done and only the packaging is behind, send us the product. If the line is yours and the shift is the problem, we come to you: that is [{ss}](/services/second-shift).
If the oil has to be made first, [toll blending](/services/toll-blending) and the fill happen at the same facility.

sections.h2: What to send for a quote
list: The safety data sheet.
The viscosity grade, or a sample.
The container and the closure, and whether it takes a spout.
Whether the fill has to hit a weight or a volume.
How many units, how often, and the date you need the first run.

sealersAndCoatings.lead: Asphalt and concrete sealers, paints and protective coatings, tints and colourants: products where the container, the colour and the timing matter as much as the fill itself.

body: A sealer or a coating is a product with a clock in it. Some form a skin where they meet air. Some settle, so the pigment sinks and the top of the tank stops matching the bottom. Some have a pot life that starts the moment two parts are brought together.
That makes the schedule part of the quote. The question is not only what the run is, but when the product will be ready, and how long it stays the product you intended.

sections.h2: Colour is a spec, not a preference
body: When colour is what your customer buys, the fill has to hold it from the first container to the last, and the next run has to match this one. Tell us how your colour is specified and how it is checked (a standard, a chip, a reading) and that becomes part of how the run is checked.

sections.h2: Solvent or water, and the sheet that says so
body: Solvent or water is the first question, and the [safety data sheet](/glossary#safety-data-sheet) answers most of the rest. It decides what can run, how the product is handled and how it is stored, so send it before the sample rather than after.
Pails, plastic and metal, take most of this work. Kits put a sealer together with its applicator in one package.

sections.h2: Two ways we can take the work
body: A plant with its own line and an empty shift can hand us the shift: [{ss}](/services/second-shift). A plant whose line is full sends the overflow here instead.

sections.h2: What to send for a quote
list: The safety data sheet, and whether it is solvent- or water-based.
How the colour is specified and checked.
Whether it skins, settles, or has a pot life.
The pail or the kit, and the lid or the outer package.
Units per run, and the date the run has to ship.

montreal.h1: Contract packaging and second shift production in greater Montreal
montreal.lead: Two ways to add output without adding a line: we run a shift on yours, or we fill and pack on ours. Both are built for plants close enough to drive to.

body: A plant runs out of capacity in one of two ways. Either the line is fine and the shifts are the limit, or the line itself is full and the orders keep arriving.

In the first case the equipment already exists and stands still for part of the day, and [{ss}](/services/second-shift) puts it back to work. In the second, nothing on your own floor will fix it in time, and the overflow has to go somewhere else. That is what our facility is for.

Overflow work is urgent by definition: it exists because an order is already waiting. Every hour the product spends on a truck is an hour of that order, and a supplier at the other end of the province spends more of them on the road than one in the same region does.

It works the same way in the other direction. Arranging a walkthrough of your line is a question of the calendar rather than of the distance, which is why we would rather look at the job than quote it blind.

sections.h2: The products we are set up for
body: They are made all over greater Montreal, in plants of every size:
list: [Cleaners](/industries/cleaners): degreasers, all-purpose, glass and floor.
[Lubricants](/industries/lubricants): oils, hydraulic and cutting fluids, greases.
[Sealers and coatings](/industries/sealers-and-coatings), and the colourants that go with them.

body: Send the product, the container and a rough run size, and we will come back with a quote. Or ask us to walk your line first: for [{ss}](/services/second-shift) that is usually the shorter path, because the shift is quoted against what is actually on your floor.

about.lead: {brand} is the operating name of {legal}. We fill, pack and blend other companies’ products: on our line, or on theirs.

body: Two things, and they are the same trade seen from two sides. [{ss}](/services/second-shift) is a production shift we run at your plant, on your line, on a shift your plant doesn’t cover. [{bn}](/services/contract-packaging) is the overflow your line can’t absorb: filled, packed and blended at ours.
Everything else on this site (the containers, the industries, the fill methods) is a description of how those two get done.

No certifications, no production figures, no square footage, no customer logos. Not because there is nothing to say, but because a claim on a marketing page can’t be checked, while a number in a quote can: it is measured against your product, your container and your run.
A client’s name appears here only with their written permission, and never as scenery.

“{bn}” reads twice. A bottleneck is the slowest step in a plant, the one everything else waits on; a bottleneck is also the neck of the bottle we fill. French gives us the same pair for nothing: goulot is both, so the name works in either language without being translated.
“{ss}” means what it says: the shift after yours, run as a service rather than sold as time.
Liquids and pastes, in the containers they are sold in. They come from a handful of trades:
list: [Cleaners](/industries/cleaners)
[Lubricants](/industries/lubricants)
[Sealers, coatings and colourants](/industries/sealers-and-coatings)

body: It starts with a question about your product, not about us: what it is, what it goes in, how many, and by when. [Getting a quote](/quote) is the short way to ask. A walkthrough of your line is the longer one, and the better one whenever the answer depends on how your floor is laid out.

privacy.h1: What this site does with your information
privacy.lead: The short version: the quote form sends an email to VKC, and nothing else on this site is watching you.

body: The quote form asks for what it takes to answer you: your name, your company, a phone number or an email address, what the product is, what it goes in, how big the run is and when you need it. Anything else you want to tell us goes in the notes.
It also records which page it was sent from, so we know whether you were reading about a walkthrough or about a service.

What you type is turned into an email and delivered to {brand} through an email delivery service. It is used to answer your request. It is not sold, rented or passed to anyone else, and there is no mailing list here to add you to.
This site has no database. Your request exists as the email we received, and nowhere else.

This site sets no advertising cookies and carries no third-party trackers, no pixels and no chat widget. Page views are counted by a measurement tool that uses no cookies and builds no profile of you, which is why nothing here asks you to accept anything.
Your choice of language is in the address of the page you are on, not in a cookie.

Quebec’s private-sector privacy law gives you the right to ask what personal information an organization holds about you, to have it corrected, and to ask that it be deleted. If you sent us a quote request and want it gone, ask us and it goes.

If what this site does with your information changes (a new form, a tracker, anything that collects more than it collects today), this page changes with it. The change gets written here rather than left to be noticed.

services.h1: Two ways to add output without adding a line
services.lead: Either we run a shift on your line, or your overflow runs on ours. Everything VKC does is one of those two, and the pages below say how each one works, who does what, and what it is priced on.

cards.secondShift: A production shift run on your own line, bought by the output.
cards.contractPackaging: The fill: your product goes into its containers at our facility.
cards.tollBlending: The batch: your formula, made here before it is filled.

body: The line is yours and already paid for; the shift is the one your plant doesn’t run. {ss} puts that equipment back to work on that shift, as a service you buy by the output. The label below says who does what.

When the line itself is full, the overflow leaves the building. {bn} takes it: filling, labelling, [kitting](/glossary#kitting) and packing, and toll blending when the product has to be made before it is packed. One quote covers the lot.

{bn} is two pages because it is two jobs. [Contract packaging](/services/contract-packaging) is the fill: the product exists and needs to get into containers. [Toll blending](/services/toll-blending) is the batch: the formula is yours, and we make the product before it is filled.

A plant whose equipment sits idle on a shift it doesn’t run wants {ss}. A plant whose line is full wants {bn}. A product that isn’t made yet wants toll blending first. The two questions below sort it out, and a walkthrough settles anything they can’t.

compare.heading: The two services, row by row, on one label

rows.label: What you send
rows.ss: Nothing: the product stays on your line
rows.bn: The product or its formula, plus the containers, closures and labels

rows.label: Who runs it
rows.ss: Our lead hand directs the shift; our crew does the work
rows.bn: Our crew, on our own line at our facility

rows.label: What comes back
rows.ss: The shift’s output, packed, documented on our QC sheets and production log
rows.bn: Filled, labelled, kitted and packed product, ready to ship

rows.label: How it is priced
rows.bn: Quoted on the job: product, container, count and date

containers.h1: The containers that have been through our line
containers.lead: Three families: bottles and jugs, pails, and kits. Each page lists what we have run, how it gets filled, and what to send us so a quote means something on the first reply.

body: The split follows the product. What pours goes in bottles and jugs. What is thick, heavy or sold to a trade goes in pails. What is sold as a set becomes a kit.

Every container on this site gets filled one of two ways. By weight, when the scale is the truth: a product sold by the kilogram, or one whose foam hides the level. To the line, when the eye is: a shelf row that has to look even. The product decides, and each container page says which way it usually goes.

The lists are a record, not a limit. A container we haven’t run is a question, not a refusal: send its name, its size and its closure, or a sample, and we will say whether it fits our line and how we would fill it.

industries.h1: Liquids and pastes, from a handful of trades
industries.lead: Cleaners, lubricants, sealers, coatings and colourants. They fill differently, they are checked differently, and each page says what changes at the line for that trade, and what to send before we quote it.

cards.cleaners: Water that foams. The fill slows or goes by weight, and the concentrate and the ready-to-use are two different runs.
cards.lubricants: Slow, clinging, and heavier cold than warm. Filling by weight when the label has to be exact, and a clean line between products.
cards.sealersCoatings: A clock in every pail. Skinning, settling and pot life set the schedule; colour is a specification, checked from the first container to the last.

sections.h2: Why the trade matters at a filling line
body: The same filler behaves differently with a foaming cleaner, a clinging oil and a coating that skins over. Knowing the trade before the first container goes under the head is what decides how the fill is set up, and how it is checked.

The three trades are where VKC is set up, not a fence around what it will look at. A product that behaves like one of them, water-based, oil-based or reactive, is worth a conversation. Send the [safety data sheet](/glossary#safety-data-sheet) and say how it pours.

sections.h2: One thing every trade sends first
body: The safety data sheet. It says what the product is, how it is handled and how it is stored, and it answers half the questions a quote would otherwise have to ask. Send it before the sample.

glossary.lead: Every term this site uses, defined the way the trade uses it, in plain words. Where a term has a page of its own, the definition points there so the page can do the explaining.

terms.def: The slowest step in a plant, the one every other step waits on, however fast the rest may be. Also the neck of a bottle, the narrow part the product passes through. VKC’s overflow service takes its name from both readings: [{bn}](/services/contract-packaging).
Everything that happens on a line between the last unit of one product and the first good unit of the next: emptying, cleaning, swapping parts, resetting the fill. A short run is mostly changeover.
Whatever seals the container: a cap, a lid, a plug, a pump or a trigger. It is quoted with the container, because it decides how the container is filled and closed on the line.
Filling and packing another company’s product, to that company’s specification, at the packager’s facility. Also called co-packing. At VKC it is the fill side of [{bn}](/services/contract-packaging).
A square-shouldered plastic jug with the handle moulded into the body, the shape many cleaners and lubricants are sold in. Filled like a bottle, palletized like a case.
The mark on a container that shows the intended level, and, on a floor, the line that fills the containers. The tagline of this site reads both ways on purpose.
Filling a container until the product reaches its fill line, rather than to a target weight. One of the two fill methods listed on the container pages.
High-density polyethylene, the stiff, opaque plastic most industrial bottles and jugs are blow-moulded from. It takes most cleaners and lubricants without complaint, which is why it is the default.
Assembling separate components, such as a filled bottle, an applicator and a leaflet, into one package that sells as a single unit. [Kits](/containers/kits) on this site means consumer kits.

The person on the floor who directs a shift: assigns the work, sets the pace, makes the calls when something drifts, signs the paperwork at the end. On a Second Shift, the lead hand is VKC’s, not the plant’s.
One batch of product made or filled together and recorded under one identifier, so that anything about it, a complaint or a question, can be traced back to the record of that run.
An open-top container with a lid and a bail handle, in plastic or metal, for the products too thick or too bulky for a bottle: sealers, coatings, greases. See [pails](/containers/pails).
The running record of a shift or a run: what was made, when, on which line, in what quantity, and what happened along the way. With the QC sheet, it is the written account of the work.
The sheet on which the checks made during a run are recorded: fills, closures, labels, counts, at the intervals the specification calls for. Quality control, written down as it happens.
A trade name for a square, stackable plastic pail with a snap-on lid, used where round pails waste pallet space. Listed among the pail families VKC has run.

The document that describes a product’s hazards, its handling and its storage, in a set format. Send it with any product that has one; it is read before the product is, and it decides how the product is stored on arrival.

VKC’s name for a production shift it runs at a customer’s plant, on the customer’s line, on a shift the plant does not cover. Our lead hand directs the shift, our crew does the work, our QC sheets and production log document it, and it is priced per unit or per shift. See [{ss}](/services/second-shift).
One continuous block of production on a line, usually one crew’s working day. A plant that runs one shift leaves its line idle for the rest of the day, which is the gap Second Shift exists to fill.
What the finished unit has to be: the fill, the closure torque, the label position, the count per case, the tolerances. The spec is the customer’s; the run is measured against it.
Making a product to a formula the customer owns, at the blender’s facility, for a processing fee. The formula stays the customer’s. See [toll blending](/services/toll-blending).
How thick a liquid is, or how much it resists flowing. It is the first thing a filler asks about, because it decides the fill method, the nozzle and the speed of the line.
Filling a container to a target weight rather than to a line, so that every unit carries the same amount of product whatever the container’s shape. The other of the two fill methods.
